name: ComicForm
iocPatterns: .rar/.zip malicious attachments with LNK or shellcode
Alternate data streams used to hide payloads
Email addresses with .ru, .by, .kz TLDs used for phishing
Reply‑to address rivet_kz@ from a Russian email service
Hidden links to animated GIF images of superheroes in attachment code
Use of digital certificates issued by SSL.com for malware signing
Malicious libraries loaded via DLL hijacking into legitimate Google Chrome update executable
keyCapabilities: Spear‑phishing attachments delivered via compromised .ru/.by/.kz email accounts
Exploitation of WinRAR zero‑day vulnerability CVE‑2025‑8088 for malicious archive delivery
Use of RAR/ZIP archives containing LNK or PowerShell payloads executed with rundll32.exe
Deployment of backdoors such as SnipBot, RustyClaw, Mythic Agent, EAGLET, and custom SNMP tools
Persistence via firmware implants (SYNful Knock) and alternate data stream techniques
Stealing configuration data from Cisco devices through Smart Install CVE‑2018‑0171 exploitation
Delivery of the FormBook infostealer via obfuscated .NET loaders (MechMatrix Pro.dll / Montero.dll)
Use of spear‑phishing links that redirect victims to cloned document storage login pages for credential theft
DLL search order hijacking to load malicious libraries into legitimate binaries such as Windows Defender and Chrome update executables
Creation of trojanized binaries (e.g., a Rufus launcher, fake ChatGPT client) to deliver final payloads
recommendedActions: Apply and maintain patches for WinRAR, including the fix for CVE‑2025‑8088
Patch Cisco IOS routers for Smart Install vulnerability (CVE‑2018‑0171) or disable the feature on unsupported devices
Block or filter spearphishing attachments and malicious RAR/ZIP files at your email gateway
Restrict execution of PowerShell scripts and prevent rundll32.exe from launching unknown DLLs
Implement detection for firmware modifications and anomalous SNMP activity
Enforce strict attachment sandboxing or block known malicious file types
Conduct targeted phishing awareness training focusing on spear‑phishing attachments and fake login pages
Monitor the integrity of signed binaries; flag certificates from suspicious issuers such as SSL.com
Deploy endpoint detection that flags DLL hijacking patterns and anomalous loader executables
Segment critical infrastructure networks to limit lateral movement of backdoor implants
campaignsText: Since its first detection in April 2025, ComicForm has maintained a consistent operational tempo focused on the Eurasian market. Victims range from mid‑size manufacturing firms to large financial institutions and critical infrastructure operators across Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and neighboring states. The actor repeatedly uses spear‑phishing attachments that bundle WinRAR archives exploiting CVE‑2025‑8088 or redirect links, followed by in‑memory DLL deployment (Montero.dll), culminating with the installation of FormBook for credential theft. Persistence mechanisms include firmware implants on network devices (SYNful Knock) and DLL hijacking within legitimate system components such as Windows Defender and Chrome update agents. ComicForm’s campaigns are typically executed over a span of weeks, indicating a well‑structured supply chain of phishing assets and custom malware capable of evading many enterprise defenses.
description: ComicForm is an emerging threat actor first observed in April 2025 that focuses on Eurasian industrial and financial organizations through sophisticated spear‑phishing campaigns coupled with zero‑day exploits such as WinRAR CVE‑2025‑8088. The group delivers a custom FormBook infostealer via obfuscated .NET loaders, employs DLL hijacking and firmware implants for persistence, and exfiltrates data while attempting to avoid detection. Although attribution remains unclear, its financial motive is evident through repeated money‑transfer and credential‑stealing operations.
goals: ComicForm’s strategic objectives appear to be dual‑faced: (1) financial gain through credential harvesting, data exfiltration, and potentially laundering stolen information; and (2) espionage or sabotage of industrial and financial assets that could provide the operator with both commercial leverage and political leverage. The actor targets a wide array of sectors—including telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, defense, government, transportation, healthcare, retail, aerospace, energy, food‑agriculture, construction, media, mining, entertainment, legal services, utilities, and hospitality—underscoring a broad operational portfolio tailored to exploit the most lucrative or strategically valuable organizations in Eurasian markets.
